text: A research report exists to let someone who wasn't in the room reach the same conclusion you did, from the same evidence, without taking your word for it. That's different from a status update and different from a polished paper. This lesson covers the structure that makes a report actually do that job.

The most common mistake is writing a report in the order the work happened, forcing the reader to reconstruct the finding from a narrative. Lead with the claim stated plainly instead, then spend the rest of the document supporting and qualifying it. Methodology — exact scale, data, training budget, number of seeds — belongs in the main body where a skeptical reader can check it, not tucked into an appendix. And uncertainty belongs right next to the number, not omitted.

A claim worth leading with states the effect size, the uncertainty around it, what exactly was held fixed between treatment and baseline, and the scope it's been tested within — not just 'sparsity helps,' but a specific number, a specific confidence interval, and an explicit note about what hasn't been tested yet.

A single number from a single run is close to uninformative, because seed-to-seed variance can be larger than many reported effects. A credible report shows the mean and spread across seeds, and ideally the individual per-seed values too, so a reader can judge for themselves whether an effect looks consistent or is being carried by one lucky run.

Next lesson covers a specific and harder case of this same discipline: presenting negative results — how to write up an approach that didn't work so it reads as genuinely useful information, not as an admission that the project failed.
